sentences.text: Mira's grandfather lived in a small wooden cabin at the very edge of the Bavarian Forest, in the south of Germany, close to the Czech border.
It was a proper Jagdhütte — a hunting cabin — that his own father had built in 1948.
It had one room, a stone fireplace, a small kitchen counter, a heavy wooden table, and two narrow beds.
There was no electricity.
There was a well outside for water.
Opa — that was what Mira called him — spent every summer here from May to September.
He was a retired forester.
He had walked these woods his whole life.
Now he was seventy-three and he walked slower, but he still walked.
Every day.
Mira was ten.
She came to stay with him for four weeks every August.
She had done this since she was five.
She loved the cabin.
She loved the smell of the pine trees.
She loved the small wooden bed with the heavy wool blanket.
She loved eating supper on the porch at dusk while the swallows dipped over the meadow.
She loved Opa, who was tall and quiet and moved through the forest like he owned it, which in a way he did — not the land, but the knowledge of it.
He knew every path.
He knew every tree that had fallen since he was young.
He knew the names of every bird by its song.
The old oak was two hours' walk from the cabin, deeper into the forest.
It was one of the first places Opa always took her when she arrived.
He said the oak was probably four hundred years old — perhaps more.
It stood in a small clearing where three deer paths met.
Its trunk was as wide as Mira's whole family standing in a ring, holding hands.
Its branches spread out overhead like a slow-motion explosion.
It had been alive when there were still bears in this forest, and wolves, and lynx.
"And it is a special oak," Opa said, on the second day of Mira's visit, as they were walking.
"It has an owl.
A tawny owl.
She lives in the hollow.
She has been there since I first came here as a boy.
I was six years old the first time my father brought me.
That was in 1957.
She was there then.
She is there now." "Opa," said Mira, patient.
"Owls do not live for sixty years.
Owls live for twenty years.
Maybe." Opa smiled.
He said, "Yes.
That is what the books say.
And yet — I know owls.
I have seen many owls in this forest.
I have written down their calls.
I have watched them raise their young.
And the owl in the oak — she is not like the other owls.
She has the same voice.
She has the same three marks over her left eye.
In sixty-eight years.
I do not have an explanation for this.
I only have what I have seen."
They came to the clearing.
The oak was there.
Mira had seen it many times before, but every year she was surprised again by how big it was.
She walked around it.
She touched the bark.
It was rough and warm.
Opa waited.
Then he pointed up at the hollow.
It was at about the height of Mira's head — a dark oval opening in the trunk, deep enough that you could not see the back of it from outside.
And inside, sitting still, was a large brown owl.
She had the round face and the dark eyes and the small tufts over her ears that Opa had described.
And, over her left eye, three small dark markings in a row.
The owl looked at them.
She was completely still.
She did not seem afraid.
She had been looked at by humans many times before.
Mira had never been this close to a wild owl before.
It was strange to be so close to something so still and so — old.
The owl was watching them with a very calm and considered look.
"Do not point at her," Opa said softly.
"Owls do not like pointing.
They read intent.
Just look.
You can talk normally.
She has heard human voices her whole life.
It does not bother her." So Mira did not point.
She just stood and looked.
She said, softly, "Hello.
I am Mira.
I have been coming to see you every summer since I was five, though I did not remember.
I am ten now." The owl did not react.
Owls do not react to what humans say to them.
But Mira felt that she had heard.
"Opa," said Mira, very quietly.
"Do you really believe it is the same one." Opa thought before he answered.
He said, "I do not really know.
What I know is: my father showed me an owl in this hollow with three marks over her left eye when I was six.
I have looked at that owl every summer of my life since.
She has the same marks.
She has the same voice.
If she is not the same owl — if it is her daughter, or her granddaughter — then somebody has been passing this hollow down for sixty-eight years.
Which is also a beautiful thing.
But it does not really matter to me which it is.
What matters is that when I come here, she is here.
And that has been true my whole life.
That is what I know.
The rest — I do not need to know."
They stayed by the oak until dusk.
Opa had brought a small thermos of coffee and a piece of bread.
They sat on a fallen log at the edge of the clearing.
They did not talk very much.
Opa told Mira the names of some of the other birds they could hear in the trees around them.
He told her which ones were species that had been in this forest for a long time, and which ones had come recently as the climate changed.
He was not sad about the changes.
He was matter of fact.
The forest was different than it had been when he was young.
Some things were gone.
Other things were arriving.
That was what a forest did.
At dusk the owl came out.
She stepped to the edge of her hollow.
She stretched.
She looked around.
Then she opened her wings — huge, silent — and she flew.
Mira watched her disappear into the dark trees.
She was silent.
Owls were built for silence.
That was why they could catch things in the dark.
Opa said, in the quiet after she had gone, "She hunts all night.
She comes back at dawn.
Now she will not be back until we are asleep.
So we go home.
Come." And they walked back to the cabin through the darkening forest, and Mira thought about the owl the whole way.
